segs.text: Section nine. The historical examples, butyrylcholinesterase and N acetyltransferase two. These were the first metabolizing enzymes in which polymorphisms were studied. Neither handles many drugs, but their genes were worked out early and a few drugs tie clearly to them. Each teaches one lesson. Butyrylcholinesterase shows how dangerous prolonged drug action can be. N acetyltransferase two shows that either direction of a phenotype can cause harm.

Butyrylcholinesterase hydrolyzes succinylcholine, a short acting muscle relaxant used in anesthesia. Succinylcholine paralyzes muscles, including the diaphragm. An extensive metabolizer clears it in about two minutes, so breathing returns quickly. A slow metabolizer keeps the drug for two to three hours, so the patient cannot breathe for that whole time unless the exposure is known. This phenotype is rare. She said, the frequency of being a slow metabolizer is only one in three thousand patients.

N acetyltransferase two is a phase two enzyme. It acetylates isoniazid, a tuberculosis drug, and it also handles procainamide. Patients are slow acetylators or fast acetylators, and both carry a risk. Slow acetylators keep isoniazid around and get peripheral nerve damage. On procainamide, slow acetylators can get drug induced lupus, because the drug is not acetylated fast enough. Fast acetylators make more of the isoniazid metabolites that cause hepatotoxicity. So you cannot assume only one phenotype is the dangerous one.

The phenotypes differ by population. About thirty to forty five percent of Caucasians are fast acetylators. About ten percent of Japanese people are slow. About eighty percent of the Middle Eastern group are slow, so that is the group to watch for slow acetylator problems.
